title: How AWS charges: the three pricing principles

kcs.statement: AWS's three fundamental cost drivers are compute, storage and outbound data transfer; inbound data transfer from the internet is generally free.
AWS pricing follows three principles: pay as you go for what you use, save when you commit to a term, and pay less per unit as your usage volume grows.

The AWS Free Tier includes always-free offers that never expire (such as Lambda's 1 million free requests per month) alongside time-limited offers for new accounts; usage above the free limits is billed at normal rates.

problem_ideas: A startup's first bill shows charges for EC2, S3 and 'DataTransfer-Out-Bytes'; which line is the one that is usually free in the other direction?
A student uploads 500 GB of video into S3 from home: which part of that is billed, the upload or the storage?
Match each slogan ('use more, pay less per GB', 'commit and save', 'no upfront cost') to the pricing principle it describes.
An account runs 800,000 Lambda requests a month: predict the request charge under the always-free tier.
A team assumes the Free Tier covers a large t3.xlarge instance; spot the mistake.
Which of these is not a fundamental AWS cost driver: compute, storage, data transfer out, number of IAM users?
